summary: Provides guidelines for extending the RTP Control Protocol (RTCP) when its basic reporting mechanisms are not enough. RTCP carries feedback between media senders and receivers. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: Rules for adding new messages to the chat between video and audio senders and receivers, so you don't break it.

subtitle: Rules for safely adding new features to the feedback channel between media senders and receivers

tldr.problem: RTP Control Protocol (RTCP) provides basic feedback between media senders and receivers, but designers keep proposing extensions that violate its core design and risk breaking compatibility.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC identifies nine categories of extension problems (trying to make RTCP reliable, turning it into a command channel, expanding it for network management, adding too much complexity) and provides a checklist for designers to follow.
tldr.outcome: RTCP extensions that respect the protocol's loose-coupling, scalable design and reuse existing mechanisms work well; those that try to remake RTCP as something else fail and harm the ecosystem.

facts.label: Extension point types
facts.value: 8 (SDES items, XR blocks, AVPF messages, APP packets, etc.)

today: RFC 5968 remains the authoritative guide for RTCP extension design. It is Informational and has not been obsoleted or updated.

sections.title: RTCP and Why Extensions Matter
sections.content:
RTP carries live media (audio and video) over unreliable networks, and RTCP is the feedback channel that runs alongside it. RTCP lets senders tell receivers how much data they sent, and receivers report back on packet loss, jitter, and delay. These reports run at a coarse granularity—every few seconds—and are best-effort (no guarantee they arrive), but they are powerful enough for applications to adapt to network conditions.

Over the years, protocol designers have proposed many RTCP extensions to add new metrics or change how the protocol works. Many of these proposals are poorly motivated or architecturally problematic. This RFC identifies the problems and offers guidance to prevent future extensions from making the same mistakes.
sections.plainLanguage: RTCP is how video senders and receivers chat about performance. It is simple and works well, but people keep trying to add things that can break it.

sections.title: What RTCP Already Offers
sections.content:
RTCP provides more functionality than most people realize. Sender reports include total packet and octet counts, allowing receivers to infer mean data rate and detect transmission pauses. Receiver reports include cumulative packet loss, jitter (smoothed variation in arrival time), and the highest sequence number seen, letting senders estimate how much data is in flight and whether the path still works. Combined with NTP and RTP timestamps in sender reports, receivers can synchronize multiple streams and senders can compute round-trip time (RTT) to each receiver.

The early feedback profile (RFC 4585) eliminates the 5-second minimum reporting interval, allowing near-instant feedback at the cost of higher RTCP bandwidth. These tools—coarse-grained reports, loose coupling, and optional early feedback—are enough to build adaptive applications for everything from VoIP to video conferencing to live streaming. Before extending RTCP, designers should ask whether existing mechanisms can already solve the problem.
sections.plainLanguage: RTCP already tells you the data rate, how many packets were lost, timing information, and RTT. People often don't realize how much it already does.

sections.title: Design Limits That Extensions Must Respect
sections.content:
RTCP is intentionally designed for scalability, not precision. It offers only occasional (coarse-grained) feedback, not per-packet feedback. It is inherently unreliable—reports can be lost, and different group members may see different views of the network state. It does not provide instant feedback (even with early feedback, only statistical guarantees). These limits are not bugs; they are features that let RTCP scale from two-party unicast sessions to groups with tens of thousands of participants.

Extensions that ignore these limits often fail. Trying to make RTCP reliable by adding acknowledgements increases complexity and delay. Turning RTCP into a command channel (telling the remote side what to do rather than reporting observations) requires reliability that RTCP cannot provide. Expanding RTCP for network management tools when the RFC notes it should carry only actionable peer-to-peer information risks growing the protocol beyond what implementers will build correctly.
sections.plainLanguage: RTCP is designed to be simple and scale to huge groups. Extensions that try to make it guaranteed, instant, or exact will fail or hurt interoperability.

sections.title: Nine Categories of Extension Mistakes
sections.content:
The RFC catalogs nine common extension pitfalls: (1) defining extensions only for unicast two-party sessions when RTP is inherently a group protocol; (2) assuming reliable, instant state synchronization when RTCP is best-effort and delayed; (3) requiring reliable delivery of reports; (4) issuing commands instead of hints; (5) expanding RTCP as a network management tool; (6) creating serious protocol complexity that discourages correct implementation; (7) introducing architectural issues (e.g., relying on eavesdropping in a secured session); (8) incompatible profile definitions without safe failure modes; and (9) not considering how extensions work with different topologies (unicast, multicast, mixers, translators).

Each mistake has real consequences. Complexity leads to buggy implementations that report incorrect data. Unicast-only extensions do not work with overlay multicast or Multipoint Control Units. Unreliable designs fail silently when RTCP packets drop, giving applications false information.
sections.plainLanguage: Extensions often go wrong by trying to make RTCP guaranteed, precise, or global when it is best-effort, coarse, and local.

sections.title: A Checklist for Extension Designers
sections.content:
The RFC provides a detailed checklist. First, ask if the extension is really needed: Can the problem be solved with existing RTCP mechanisms? Is it truly a network condition, or a lazy implementation? Does it apply broadly, or only to one use case? Second, check applicability: Will it work everywhere RTP runs, or only in specific networks? Does it scale gracefully with group size? Third, consider the design: How does it interact with other RTCP components? Does it work with all profiles and topologies? How does it degrade when packets drop or latency increases?

For the implementation, the RFC advises: Prefer reusing existing standards over inventing new metrics. Avoid signalling information that can be inferred from other values or their evolution. Use soft reliability (inferring receipt from behavior changes, like a video codec switching codecs). Choose the right extension point: SDES items for source description, XR blocks for metrics, AVPF feedback messages for transport-layer hints, or new RTCP packet types only when nothing else fits. Keep the design simple so implementers will build it correctly.
sections.plainLanguage: Before adding to RTCP, check if you really need to, if it works for everyone, and if it can be simple enough that people will implement it right.

sections.title: Security and Deployment Concerns
sections.content:
Extensions must be careful not to leak sensitive information (privacy) or disrupt RTCP's carefully tuned congestion control. RTCP timers have been designed to scale from two-party sessions to thousands of participants without causing congestion or denial of service. Extensions that change the timing algorithms risk breaking that property. Extensions that change where feedback is sent must prevent denial-of-service attacks against third parties, typically by authenticating the signalling that enables them.

The RFC notes that as of 2010, many deployed implementations do not even correctly implement baseline RTCP despite its precise specification and sample code. Adding more complexity makes this problem worse. The best extensions are those that extend minimally, work with existing RTP topologies and profiles, and let applications use what already exists before reaching for something new.
sections.plainLanguage: Extensions should not leak private data, break the careful balance that lets RTCP scale, or be so complex that no one implements them right.
